from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(reader.pages))

parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(reader.pages,1):

 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n'+text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))

strengths: AiT offers a potentially useful architectural combination: a compact shared memory, sparse patch selection across a batch, and associative retrieval integrated into a Vision Transformer. This provides a concrete approach to sharing information across images.

Table 1 reports meaningful improvements over the corresponding ViT configurations. AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, with parameters increasing from 14.9M to 15.8M. Improvements also appear for the Base configuration.

The component ablations provide useful evidence. Removing the bottleneck reduces CIFAR-10 accuracy from 83.34% to 75.40%, while replacing Hopfield retrieval with cross-attention reduces it to 81.03%. These results support the usefulness of the proposed combination under the reported training conditions.

The manuscript includes memory-initialization and temperature studies, attention visualizations, and energy measurements. Reporting three-run means and providing an extensive hyperparameter appendix are helpful reproducibility efforts.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is materially underspecified for a model that shares state across images. Section 4.1 pools patches across a batch, and Equation 4 carries memory across steps, but evaluation-time memory updates, freezing/resetting, and batch construction are not explained. Predictions could depend on batch composition and, if memory persists, evaluation order. Moreover, k=512 exceeds the 64 patches in a single CIFAR image, requiring an unstated inference rule. These omissions limit interpretation of the comparisons with standard ViT inference.

The central complexity-invariance claim is not supported by the described computation. Section 4.2 computes scores between every memory slot and every input patch before applying top-k; fixed bottleneck capacity therefore does not eliminate input-size dependence. Projection costs also depend on embedding dimension, and the complete AiT retains quadratic per-image self-attention. Parameter counts alone, without FLOPs, runtime, or peak-memory scaling measurements, do not substantiate the broader efficiency claims.

The retrieval algorithm and its claimed distinction from attention need a more precise technical foundation. Equation 8 specifies an argmin without giving the actual update rule, iteration count, stopping criterion, or differentiation procedure. For the usual continuous Hopfield energy in Equation 7, the standard fixed-point update is softmax attention with memory serving as both keys and values. Consequently, the assertion that retrieval fundamentally differs from attention is overstated, and the cross-attention replacement ablation is insufficiently specified to resolve the distinction.

The load component of the balance loss has an unresolved gradient issue. Equation 5 counts entries satisfying A>0: for the defined softmax attention, these counts are constant; if masked attention is intended, the hard counts are piecewise constant and provide zero gradient almost everywhere. No surrogate or gradient estimator is described. This does not invalidate the differentiable importance component, but it undermines the stated role of the load regularizer.

The specialization evidence does not isolate the proposed explanation. Figures 8–9 show changes during training without a matched comparison excluding the balance loss. Figure 7 also appears inconsistent with its percentage interpretation: many light-blue heads have medians around 47–49 patches out of 65, which does not support the accompanying claim of 50% or fewer interactions. Attention concentration and increasing patch diversity provide weaker evidence than the claimed emergence of specialized priors.

The empirical conclusions require qualification: relational accuracy is 67.74%, below Coordination's 73.43% and CNN+RN's 81.07%, despite strong non-relational results. The main tables omit variability across the three runs. A smaller, readily correctable reporting issue is the learning-rate discrepancy between Section 5.1 (1e-5) and Table 6 (1e-4). The promising classification gains warrant further consideration, but the unresolved algorithmic definitions, inference protocol, and efficiency claims determine my weak-reject recommendation.
